tts_summary: Here's your midday Fed update for October 7th, 2026. The Federal Reserve just released the minutes from the September 15th and 16th FOMC meeting, and while there were no major surprises, there are some important takeaways traders need to digest. First, the big headline: most participants felt that only one more rate hike would be appropriate by year-end. The Fed raised rates 25 basis points at that September meeting, bringing the target range to 3.75 to 4 percent. But here's the context that matters — that consensus for one more hike was formed before we got the soft September jobs report and the weaker August PCE and JOLTs data. So the bar for that final hike may already be shifting. On inflation, the tone is unambiguously hawkish. Officials said inflation remains elevated, they have not seen sufficient progress in recent months, and they explicitly assessed inflation risks as skewed to the upside — with some saying those risks have grown more tilted in the wrong direction recently. Core services ex-housing is still hot. Core goods inflation is still elevated. And the AI buildout is actually adding to cost pressures — higher energy, higher transportation, higher input costs — even as tariff effects are fading. A few participants flagged that software and portfolio management fees made outsized contributions to recent PCE readings, but those may ease with upcoming methodology changes from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, so watch that. On financial conditions, the picture is more balanced. Despite rising longer-term Treasury yields, officials said financial conditions still appear supportive of growth. Credit is broadly available, corporate issuance is strong, and lending standards have eased. Stock market gains are also supporting consumer spending, particularly at the high end. Labor markets were described as stable and close to maximum employment. One under-the-radar note worth flagging: a few officials raised the issue of Treasury market stress. They suggested the Fed should strengthen its strategy and tools to handle potential market dysfunction — while keeping its footprint in the Treasury market limited. That's a subtle but important signal that officials are at least thinking about tail risks in fixed income. Bottom line: these minutes lean hawkish on inflation, confirm one more hike is the base case for year-end, but incoming soft data could change that math. Stay alert to any Fed speakers this week who may update their views in light of the data that dropped after this meeting.
